Adult black-stripe sweepers are known to attain an ultimate standard length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm], a size that is modest relative to some larger congeners, yet represents a considerable investment in somatic growth over the species’ lifespan. The largest individuals collected in reef surveys typically achieve this maximum body size, which provides a benchmark against which other demographic parameters are assessed. Associated with this terminal length is an ultimate wet weight of 52 grams [Wwi = 52 grams], a value derived from length–weight relationships established for the population. This adult mass reflects the accumulation of both somatic and gonadal tissues in sexually mature fish and serves as a basis for comparing energetic demands across different life stages. The relatively compact body plan of Pempheris schwenkii suggests a life history tuned to the structural complexity of the shallow coral reef environments it inhabits, where maneuverability and the ability to seek refuge in narrow crevices likely confer a selective advantage over absolute body size.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species is marked by the achievement of a standard length at puberty of 5.3 cm [Lp = 5.3 cm], a size that is typically attained within the first year of growth. Corresponding to this length is a wet weight at puberty of 2.32 grams [Wwp = 2.32 grams], indicating that substantial somatic development must occur before gonadal recrudescence is initiated. Field collections have consistently shown that individuals below this size threshold possess undifferentiated or immature gonads, whereas those exceeding it display active gametogenesis. The transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive investment is a critical ecological juncture, as it requires that sufficient energy reserves have been accumulated to support the metabolic costs of spawning activity. The relatively early puberty in terms of absolute length suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes an early onset of reproduction, potentially as a bet-hedging tactic against unpredictable mortality in the reef environment.

Reproduction in black-stripe sweepers begins with the production of small, pelagic eggs that are released into the water column during spawning events. The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of a newly fertilized ovum, has been estimated from egg diameter measurements at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This extraordinarily low birth mass is consistent with the production of numerous, small oocytes, a pattern common among broadcast-spawning teleosts that rely on high fecundity to offset high rates of larval mortality. The eggs are transparent and yolk-laden, providing the endogenous nutrients required during the initial lecithotrophic phase before the mouth opens and the yolk-sac larva must transition to exogenous feeding. The energetic investment per offspring is minimal, yet the cumulative reproductive output of a single female over a spawning season can be substantial, reflecting a life-history strategy that emphasizes quantity over individual offspring provisioning.

Longevity records for Pempheris schwenkii, based on the oldest individual caught during extensive reef sampling, indicate a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] under the prevailing water temperatures of the study region at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This estimate was derived from fish maintained under natural conditions at a mean annual temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a thermal regime typical of tropical coral reef ecosystems. It is probable that the true maximum lifespan of this species is somewhat greater than the documented catch, as the oldest individuals may be underrepresented in trap and net surveys due to behavioral or habitat biases. Nevertheless, a six-year lifespan places the species within the range of values reported for other small-to-medium-sized reef fishes, suggesting a moderate pace of life. This longevity, combined with the early age at sexual maturity, implies that most individuals have multiple reproductive opportunities across several breeding seasons, a classic iteroparous strategy that buffers against year-to-year variability in recruitment success.

A comparative perspective on the life history of Pempheris schwenkii reveals several notable features when examined against other members of the family Pempheridae. The ultimate body length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] is close to the upper end of the size spectrum for the genus, with some congeneric species maturing at considerably smaller sizes. The standard length at puberty of 5.3 cm [Lp = 5.3 cm] represents roughly 35 percent of the ultimate length, a proportional threshold that is relatively consistent across sweepers and suggests a conserved developmental schedule. The wet weight at puberty of 2.32 grams [Wwp = 2.32 grams], as an absolute value, is modest but sufficient to support the energetic demands of gonad development in a fish that relies on a planktivorous diet of zooplankton. The ultimate wet weight of 52 grams [Wwi = 52 grams] represents a substantial gain from the 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] birth mass, representing a near hundred-thousand-fold increase in mass over the course of a 6-year lifespan  in waters averaging 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This dramatic ontogenetic scaling of body mass underscores the efficiency of marine food webs in supporting the rapid growth of teleost fishes during their early life stages.
